context:
Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a pattern scientists call the urban heat island. The causes are not mysterious. Asphalt and dark roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after sunset, so city nights cool far less than rural ones. Buildings block the wind that would otherwise carry warm air away, and engines, air conditioners and factories add heat of their own. Trees, by contrast, cool their surroundings twice over: their leaves shade the ground, and the water they release through their leaves absorbs heat as it evaporates.

Some cities have begun to treat this as a planning problem rather than a fact of life. Painting roofs white, replacing parking lots with parks and planting street trees all lower surface temperatures, sometimes dramatically. Yet these measures are unevenly distributed. In many cities, wealthier neighborhoods have more tree cover than poorer ones, which means the residents least able to afford air conditioning are often the ones living on the hottest streets. Cooling a city, then, is not only a technical question; it is also a question of who benefits.
prompt: Does the passage suggest that planting street trees in poorer neighborhoods could help with an unfairness the author describes?
rationale: Trees cool streets and poorer areas have fewer trees and less air conditioning, so yes.

Nadia had watched her grandfather repair clocks for most of her life, but she had never been allowed to touch the tools. They lay on the felt in the same order every evening: the tweezers, the tiny screwdrivers, the loupe he screwed into his eye like a monocle. On the night he handed her the tweezers without a word, she understood that something had changed, though she could not have said what.

"The balance wheel," he said, pointing. His hands, she noticed, were shaking more than they used to. She lifted the wheel the way she had seen him do a thousand times, holding her breath as if the air itself might knock it loose. It took her twenty minutes to seat it. He did not help, and he did not hurry her. When the clock finally began to tick, he only nodded and turned off the lamp, but at the door he paused and rested his hand on her shoulder for a moment longer than he needed to.

The next evening, the tools were laid out on her side of the bench.
prompt: Does the passage suggest that the grandfather is beginning to pass his craft on to Nadia?
rationale: He hands her the tools, lets her work unaided, and next day lays them on her side of the bench.

context:
To the school board:

Starting classes at 8:45 instead of 7:30 would improve our students' lives. Sleep researchers have found that teenagers' internal clocks shift later during adolescence, so many students simply cannot fall asleep before eleven. At 7:30, they arrive having slept six or seven hours instead of the eight to ten that doctors recommend. Tired students learn less and are more likely to fall ill. I have taught first period for twelve years, and I can tell you that my students are noticeably more alert after lunch than at dawn. Last year, a neighboring district moved its start time later, and its football team went on to win the regional championship.

Critics say later starts will disrupt bus schedules and after-school jobs. These are real costs, and the board should plan for them. But a schedule that works against our students' biology is a cost too, and it is one we pay every single morning.

A first-period teacher
prompt: Is the result of the neighboring district's football team strong evidence that later start times improve students' learning?
rationale: A sports win says nothing reliable about learning; it is irrelevant evidence.

context:
For centuries, sailors could find their latitude easily by measuring the height of the sun or the Pole Star above the horizon. Longitude was another matter. Because the Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour, a navigator who knew both the local time and the time at his home port could calculate how far east or west he had traveled. Local time was easy to find from the sun. The difficulty was carrying home-port time across an ocean. Pendulum clocks, the most accurate of the era, were useless on a rolling deck, and changes in temperature made metal parts expand and throw the mechanism off.

In the eighteenth century, a carpenter-turned-clockmaker named John Harrison spent decades building sea clocks that could keep time through storms and heat. Many experts of the day favored an astronomical method instead, using the moon's position against the stars, and some of them doubted that any machine could be trusted. Harrison's fourth timekeeper eventually proved accurate on a voyage to the Caribbean, and within a few generations marine chronometers became standard equipment on ocean-going ships.
prompt: According to the reasoning in the passage, if a ship's local noon came two hours after noon at its home port, had the ship moved about thirty degrees of longitude?
rationale: The Earth turns fifteen degrees per hour, and 2 × 15 = 30.

Some people say that a town library is a luxury in an age when every phone holds a search engine. I would ask them to spend one afternoon at ours. They would see a retired mechanic learning to write a resume on a public computer. They would see two sisters, newly arrived in this country, practicing English with a volunteer at the corner table. They would see a high-school student who has no quiet place at home doing her chemistry homework until closing time. None of these people came for a search engine. They came for a place that is warm, free and open to everyone, a place that asks nothing of them except that they return what they borrow.

When the council votes next month on whether to cut the library's hours, it will be voting on more than a budget line. It will be deciding whether those afternoons continue. I hope its members will visit before they decide.
